title: Interfacial orbital torques excite nanoscale terahertz magnons
authors: Harshita Devda, Peter M. Oppeneer, Ulrich Nowak
abstract: Exchange-dominated magnons in nanometer-thick ferromagnets extend to the terahertz regime through thickness quantization of perpendicular standing spin-wave (PSSW) modes. While interfacial spin-orbit torques (SOTs) have been shown to enable the excitation of such modes, the microscopic origin of the interfacial driving torque remains unclear. In particular, the coexistence of spin and orbital currents complicates the understanding. Here, we develop and use an atomistic framework that explicitly resolves interfacial symmetries and separates spin and orbital torque contributions. Exploiting a trilayer geometry for a thin ferromagnet sandwiched between non-magnetic layers, where the symmetry-controlled polarity of the interfacial torque produces mode-selective magnon excitation as observed in the recent experiment of Salikhov et al. Nature Phys. 19, 529 (2023), we disentangle the different interfacial torque contributions. By decomposing the torque into magnetization-even (field-like) and magnetization-odd components, we identify the field-like torque as the dominant contribution responsible for the excitation. Crucially, isolating orbital and spin contributions reveals that the interfacial orbital torque provides the primary channel for the efficient excitation of exchange-dominated THz magnons in thin ferromagnets. Our results establish a microscopic basis for symmetry-engineered control of confined terahertz spin dynamics in magnetic multilayers.
summary: This paper theoretically investigates the mechanism driving terahertz magnon excitation in thin magnetic multilayers. By developing an atomistic framework, the authors successfully decompose the complex interfacial spin-orbit torque into its constituent spin and orbital parts. They conclude that the orbital torque, specifically its field-like component, is the dominant microscopic mechanism enabling efficient, symmetry-controlled excitation of these confined THz spin waves.
main_problem: The study aims to resolve the microscopic origin of the interfacial driving torque responsible for exciting terahertz (THz) magnons in nanometer-thick ferromagnets, particularly due to the complexity of coexisting spin and orbital currents.
main_result: The research identifies the interfacial orbital torque as the primary channel for efficiently exciting exchange-dominated THz magnons, with the field-like component being the dominant torque contribution.
method: The authors developed an atomistic framework, using first-principles calculations (Kubo formalism) and atomistic spin-dynamics simulations, to explicitly separate and analyze spin and orbital torque contributions.
model_or_system: The system involves thin ferromagnets (e.g., Co) sandwiched between non-magnetic layers, forming trilayers (NM/FM/NM). The model utilizes an effective Heisenberg Hamiltonian augmented by a Spin-Orbit Torque (SOT) term.
key_observables: Excitation of perpendicular standing spin-wave (PSSW) modes in the THz regime, and the spectral power densities ($	ilde{q}(f), 	ilde{g}(f)$) derived from the magnetization dynamics.
important_parameters: THz pulse amplitude ($\sim 10^8$ V/m), film thickness ($N_z$ layers), and the separation of torque into field-like (M-even) and anti-damping-like (M-odd) components.
main_assumptions: The SOT effective fields are assumed to remain close to their static values over the THz excitation timescale, and the orbital torque contribution is localized at the interfaces.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the schematic of symmetric/asymmetric trilayers under THz pulses, showing how SOTs support different PSSW modes. Subsequent figures compare mode excitation using different torque components (M-even vs. M-odd) and highlight the role of the orbital torque.
paper_structure: The paper progresses by establishing the physical problem (unclear torque origin), detailing the theoretical framework (atomistic decomposition of SOT), presenting the simulation results (analyzing mode excitation based on torque components), and concluding with the identification of the orbital torque as the key driver.
why_interesting: This work provides a detailed, atomistic, and symmetry-controlled understanding of how interfacial coupling mechanisms (orbital torques) can be engineered to control quantum dynamics (THz magnons) in condensed matter systems, which is highly relevant to open quantum systems and spintronics.
